question.value: To what extent does supernova feedback influence the chemical evolution and molecular complexity of protostellar cores located within a supernova remnant?

evidence.quote: However, the extent to which supernovae influence their chemical evolution remains unclear.
This study represents the first observational attempt to characterize the chemical evolution of protostellar cores located within a SNR.

findings_qualitative.value: First detection of hot molecular cores (HC1 and HC2) in a supernova-feedback region, associated with Class I intermediate-mass protostars inside the X-ray shell of RX J1713.7-3946.

evidence.quote: We report the first detection of hot molecular cores in a supernova remnant using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array.
The detected hot cores (HC1 and HC2) are located inside the X-ray shell of the young supernova remnant RX J1713.7$-$3946, and both sources are associated with Class I intermediate-mass protostars.

findings_qualitative.value: Column density ratios of COMs (HCOOCH3/CH3OH, CH3OCH3/CH3OH, CH3CHO/CH3OH), deuterated methanol (CH2DOH/CH3OH), and S- and N-bearing molecules (OCS/CH3OH, C2H5CN/CH3CN) in HC1 are indistinguishable from hot cores/corinos in typical star-forming environments.

evidence.quote: Despite being located within a supernova-feedback region, the column density ratios of complex organic molecules (HCOOCH$_3$/CH$_3$OH, CH$_3$OCH$_3$/CH$_3$OH, and CH$_3$CHO/CH$_3$OH), a deuterated molecule (CH$_2$DOH/CH$_3$OH), and sulfur- and nitrogen-bearing species (OCS/CH$_3$OH and C$_2$H$_5$CN/CH$_3$CN) in HC1 are indistinguishable from those observed in hot cores/corinos in more typical star-forming environments.

findings_qualitative.value: Isotope ratios (12C/13C and 34S/33S) in HC1 are consistent with the local ISM, indicating no significant modification by the supernova event.

evidence.loc: Molecular column densities and gas temperatures
evidence.quote: These values are consistent with those in the local ISM (cite: Yan23), suggesting that the isotope ratios in HC1 have not been significantly modified by the supernova event.

findings_qualitative.value: Survival of molecular complexity in HC1 is explained by short exposure time (< 1000 yr) near the outer edge of the supernova shell and/or magnetic field shielding that keeps the effective cosmic-ray ionization rate below 10^-15 s^-1.

evidence.quote: The elapsed time since the onset of exposure to high-energy particles and photons may be too short for the chemical composition of the hot core to be significantly altered, and/or the hot-core region may be shielded by magnetic fields amplified by supernova feedback, which could suppress the penetration of enhanced cosmic rays.
Our calculations show that, for an ionization rate below 10$^{-15}$ s$^{-1}$, the gas-phase molecular abundances do not change significantly over a timescale of $\sim$1000 years.

claims.hypothesis: Protostellar cores located inside the X-ray shell of the supernova remnant RX J1713.7-3946 harbor hot molecular cores.
claims.experiment: Conduct high-spatial-resolution (~0.4''-0.5'') ALMA Band 6 and Band 7 continuum and spectral line observations toward two outflow-hosting fields (Peak D and Peak C) in RX J1713.7-3946, and compile 3-500 um SEDs.
claims.result: Detected compact (< 500 au), dense (n_H2 ~ 1-2 x 10^7 cm^-3), high-temperature (T_rot > 100 K) molecular gas rich in COMs and continuum peaks with bolometric luminosities of 260 L_sun (HC1) and 230 L_sun (HC2).
claims.finding: HC1 and HC2 are hot molecular cores associated with intermediate-mass Class I protostars inside a supernova-feedback region.

evidence.quote: Excitation analyses of HC1 reveal rotational temperatures exceeding 100 K for many molecular species.
Based on these characteristics, we interpret these two sources as hot molecular cores associated with intermediate-mass Class I protostars.

claims.hypothesis: Supernova feedback in RX J1713.7-3946 has significantly altered the chemical composition, deuterium fractionation, and isotopic ratios of the hot core HC1 compared to typical star-forming regions.
claims.experiment: Derive column densities, rotational temperatures, and abundance ratios of COMs, N- and S-bearing molecules, CH2DOH, and 13C/34S/33S isotopologues in HC1 and compare them with literature hot cores and hot corinos.
claims.result: Abundance ratios (HCOOCH3/CH3OH, CH3OCH3/CH3OH, CH3CHO/CH3OH, OCS/CH3OH, C2H5CN/CH3CN), deuterium fractionation (CH2DOH/CH3OH ~ 0.5%), and isotope ratios (12C/13C = 56-69, 34S/33S = 3-6) show no significant deviation from typical hot cores/corinos and local ISM values.
claims.finding: The chemical composition, deuterium fractionation, and isotope ratios of HC1 have not been significantly altered by supernova feedback.

evidence.quote: As shown in the figure, the COM composition of RX1713 HC1 does not show any significant deviation from those of other hot cores/corinos.
The CH$_2$DOH/CH$_3$OH ratio in HC1 is approximately 0.5$\%$ and does not show any significant difference from those measured in other objects with similar luminosities.

The above comparisons suggest that the chemical compositions of major COMs and nitrogen- and sulfur-bearing molecules in HC1, as well as the degree of CH$_3$OH deuterium fractionation, have not been significantly altered by supernova feedback.

claims.hypothesis: Gas-phase COMs in HC1 can survive for ~1000 yr under supernova feedback if the exposure duration is short and/or cosmic-ray penetration is suppressed below an ionization rate of 10^-15 s^-1.
claims.experiment: Run pseudo-time-dependent gas-phase astrochemical simulations with the Rokko code at n(H2) = 10^7 cm^-3 and T = 150 K for ionization rates zeta = 10^-17 to 10^-14 s^-1.
claims.result: Gas-phase COM abundances remain nearly unchanged over a 10^3 yr timescale when the ionization rate is below 10^-15 s^-1.
claims.finding: Recent onset of exposure (< 1000 yr) at the outer edge of the SNR shell and/or magnetic field shielding of cosmic rays can explain the unaltered chemical composition of HC1.

evidence.quote: Our calculations show that, for an ionization rate below 10$^{-15}$ s$^{-1}$, the gas-phase molecular abundances do not change significantly over a timescale of $\sim$1000 years.

why_this_data.value: High-spatial-resolution ALMA observations toward Peak D and Peak C in RX J1713.7-3946 were chosen because both fields exhibit CO bipolar outflow signatures indicating ongoing star formation inside a young SNR shell.

evidence.quote: Chemical analyses of compact, dense, and high-temperature regions associated with protostars are essential for understanding the impact of supernova feedback on the chemical evolution of COMs in star- and planet-forming regions.
The Peak D field includes a source that exhibits signatures of a bipolar molecular outflow traced by CO gas in the ALMA archival data (ID: 2017.1.01406.S).
The presence of protostellar outflows is a good indicator of ongoing star formation.

referee_caveats_inferred: The non-LTE excitation analysis reported in Table 3 (column N_non-LTE(X)) is not described in the text or appendices (neither the radiative transfer code nor the assumed kinetic temperatures, collider densities, and collision rates are stated).

Beam dilution is not explicitly corrected in the rotation diagram analysis for compact species whose deconvolved sizes (< 0.21''-0.26'') are smaller than the 0.50'' extraction aperture and 0.54'' convolved beam.
